name: Brown Yellow
lede: Brown yellow is a plain compound name for a dark, dull gold, and in our sources it is a descriptive phrase, not the name of a pigment or a history.

sections.title: A name made of two words
sections.body:
The swatch here, #B29705, comes from the 2010 xkcd color survey [1]. No older chart in our library carries the name, and Dark Gold is a near duplicate only 2.0 units away [1]. The nearest established name in our app is [[mustard]], about 6.5 units off [1]. [[ochre]] is another near neighbor, and the library lists Brown Yellow as its close match [1].

So who coined it is undocumented. The books use *brown, yellow* mostly as a list of two separate colors, and sometimes as a hyphenated description of a mineral. Goethite, the iron oxide behind yellow ochre, shifts from green-yellow to brown-yellow as its particles grow larger [2]. Ozocerite, a mineral wax, is described as brown-yellow [3]. The Pigment Compendium also uses Yellow-Brown as one of its own classes of colors [4].

The nearest ordinary history is the earth yellows. Yellow ochres built on goethite are among the oldest pigments, and researchers have identified them in French cave paintings [2].

sections.title: Where the shade turns up in words
sections.body:
Pastoureau describes medieval white wool that was bleached in the fields and gradually turned grayish brown, yellow or ecru [5]. *Khaki* is a mixed shade between brown, yellow, grey and green; it comes from a Hindustani word for earth color, not from the French name of the persimmon [6]. Both are close in spirit to this color, a [[khaki]]-like warmth with more yellow [6].

A warning for the eye: the swatch is a dark gold, not a mud. Screens show it at a lightness near 63, and next to [[mustard]] it reads as the same family, only duller [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This color appears in 70 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.3 per cent, and it is more common than 54 per cent of the named colors [7]. Within a painting it most often plays an accent, in 82 per cent of 68 paintings [7]. It peaks in the 1900s, with 9 of 1,674 paintings, 1.7 times the expected rate [7].

The most striking pattern is regional: 10 of the 721 Indian paintings in the archive match it, 4.4 times the baseline, and the Rajput school is 10.7 times over [7]. [[painter:luis-melendez|Meléndez]] uses it in 4 of his 39 works here [7]. It keeps company with Mustard and Olive above all [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [7].
